papers.abstract: We study a constrained sequential decision problem for detecting regions of interest from noisy online measurements collected by a team of energy-constrained mobile sensors. The sensor motion is restricted to a precomputed set of feasible paths that satisfy mobility constraints, limited available energy by requiring return to charging stations, and avoidance of known obstacles. We cast the resulting active path selection as a multi-armed bandit problem and propose an iterative search algorithm that adaptively assigns paths using confidence bounds computed from the collected data. We also propose a graph-based method to construct low-cardinality path covers under the team's constraints. We establish finite-time and anytime probabilistic correctness guarantees for the proposed algorithm, derive non-asymptotic upper bounds on the times required to detect all regions of interest and to label all nodes, and show that these bounds match algorithm-independent lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of problem instances. Using numerical simulations, we illustrate the behavior of the proposed approach and the effect of path redundancy and team size on search performance.
bullets: Models constrained path selection from noisy online measurements as a multi-armed bandit problem.

Constructs low-cardinality path covers while respecting mobility, energy, charging, and obstacle constraints.
Provides finite-time and anytime correctness guarantees plus non-asymptotic detection and labeling bounds.
Simulations examine how path redundancy and team size affect search performance.

papers.abstract: Video world models generate future visual observations from camera or action inputs, with the goal of synthesizing persistent 3D worlds that can be explored across time and space. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate short interactions or rely on camera trajectories fixed before generation. The performance of video world models under long-horizon exploration with extensive camera motion remains under-explored. We introduce WorldProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that uses a goal-conditioned multimodal agent to adapt camera actions online during generation. WorldProbe comprises 164 test cases across four probing families. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, we generate more than 1,600 rollouts totaling approximately 800 minutes, with horizons up to 180 seconds. Our evaluation across four dimensions reveals both the degradation of local measures and the emergence of long-range inconsistencies. We find that recent models sustain visual and content quality for longer, while long-range memory and evolution remain weak. These results expose a gap between locally stable generation and persistent world consistency that is largely missed by existing benchmarks. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/Untitled-W/WorldProbe.
bullets: Existing benchmarks largely miss failures under long-horizon exploration with online camera motion.

papers.abstract: Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have shown strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions. In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy lets these agents search over modular and editable robot programs. However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail. Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved. We introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three components. First, a hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, learned from embodied data and online task solving. Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities. Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties. RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and $π_{0.5}$ on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. We further show that the knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with its size. Project page: https://roboauto-ai.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the limitation of refining robot programs from execution feedback without resolving underlying physical uncertainties.
Uses a hierarchical knowledge base covering executable skills, object affordances, spatial relations, and action effects.
Grounds this knowledge in the current scene by identifying relevant objects and action-critical quantities.
Employs multi-stage planning and self-designed experiments to verify expected effects and distinguish competing hypotheses.

Reports strong results across simulated and real-robot benchmarks, including an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and improved long-horizon performance; knowledge transfers across simulators and embodiments.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.
bullets: Addresses article-isolated, black-box sentiment prediction in high-stakes financial applications.
Uses SEC 10-K-derived knowledge graphs to provide company profiles or relevance-ranked factual triples as context.
Works with any causal LLM without updating model weights and with nearly no added computational cost.
Attributes sentiment scores to article sentences and retrieved facts for inspectable, human-reviewable evidence.
Simulations show consistent portfolio-performance gains over a state-of-the-art baseline.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. First, expert demonstrations show only one behavior per scenario, so the model cannot learn alternative valid behaviors and, in turn, cannot adapt to user-specified preferences at test time. Second, noise or ambiguity in these demonstrations can produce inconsistent, unreliable supervision for the end-to-end models. Driving is inherently multi-modal: multiple different behaviors can be valid responses to the same scene, and this diversity arises largely from speed rather than path. We introduce a planning paradigm that learns the path through imitation while scoring a set of candidate speeds across multiple criteria with a learned function supervised by physically grounded safety constraints. We realize this paradigm as Closed-Loop Aware Planning for Autonomous Driving (CLAP-AD), a plug-in planning head that integrates with existing end-to-end driving models and, to our knowledge, is the first to enable explicit test-time control over their speed selection without speed-conditioned training. On Bench2Drive-Speed, CLAP-AD sets a new state of the art Speed-Adherence Score of 82.53, topping TFv6, the strongest baseline on this metric, by 12.9 points while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance. On Bench2Drive, it improves driving score by +28.5 and +32.7 over UniAD and VAD, and on NAVSIM v2, built on real-world driving data, EPDMS by +6.1 over its backbone. Project page: https://clap-ad.github.io
bullets: Addresses limited behavioral diversity and noisy supervision in open-loop imitation learning.
Learns paths through imitation while scoring candidate speeds using multiple criteria and physically grounded safety constraints.
Works as a plug-in planning head for existing end-to-end driving models without speed-conditioned training.
Achieves state-of-the-art speed adherence on Bench2Drive-Speed and improves driving performance on Bench2Drive and NAVSIM v2.
Scope: the approach focuses on behavioral multimodality arising primarily from speed rather than path.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the CLAP-AD planning head. The architecture consists of an Ego-Path block that takes ego detection and motion queries as input and predicts a feasible driving path. The Collision block encodes surrounding agents’ detection and motion queries, fuses them with the predicted path representation, and uses learned collision queries to produce collision scores. Similarly, the Traffic Light and Stop Sign blocks employ dedicated queries that attend to their respective detection features together with the path embedding to generate their speed scores.

Figure 5. Driving Score versus Comfort on the 220 Bench2Drive routes. Comfort falls as Driving Score rises; the dashed line is a least-squares fit over the methods shown. papers.abstract: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals. Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning. To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning. With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.

papers.abstract: Chest computed tomography (CT) reports generated by large language models (LLMs) can describe positive findings that lack localized evidence in the scan. We propose EviGround-CT to verify these findings after report generation. A deterministic extractor identifies positive finding sentences, and a 3D grounding model predicts an evidence mask for each sentence. Using the full sentence retains anatomical location, laterality, and descriptive modifiers in the grounding query. We evaluate report generation on CT-RATE, and grounding and verification on a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset. Using the available annotations, sentence-grounded verification raises evidence-supported precision (ESP) from 0.263 to 0.365 across 137 extracted in-scope positives, compared with category conditioning. The corresponding unsupported positive finding rate falls from 0.737 to 0.635. The paired case-level bootstrap ESP difference is +0.102 (95% confidence interval: [0.028, 0.181]). The predicted masks associate individual report statements with spatial evidence that can be inspected alongside the CT.

Extracts positive finding sentences deterministically and uses each full sentence as the grounding query.
A 3D grounding model predicts an inspectable evidence mask for every statement.
On annotated cases, evidence-supported precision increased from 0.263 to 0.365, while unsupported positives decreased from 0.737 to 0.635.
Evaluated on CT-RATE and a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset; scope is limited to available annotations and in-scope positives.

papers.abstract: While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that vision and language models converge toward compatible latent geometries, recovering class-level correspondences between unpaired modalities without cross-modal supervision remains challenging. Existing relational matching methods compare within-modality similarity kernels directly, although the same semantic structure may be represented through different numerical parameterizations across modalities. We propose RankAlign, a rank-based normalization strategy for class-level unpaired vision-language matching. RankAlign transforms each within-modality similarity kernel into an ordinal relational representation before permutation matching, while leaving the correspondence space and matching solver unchanged. The resulting representation is invariant to strictly increasing reparameterizations of similarity values while preserving the ordinal structure used for matching. We provide exact-recovery and stability guarantees that characterize correspondence recovery under both exact and partial ordinal agreement. Experiments across diverse frozen vision and language encoders and multiple datasets demonstrate improved and more stable class-level correspondence recovery, including under label corruption and domain shift.
bullets: Addresses class-level correspondence recovery between unpaired vision and language modalities without cross-modal supervision.
Transforms within-modality similarity kernels into ordinal representations before permutation matching, without changing the matching space or solver.
Is invariant to strictly increasing reparameterizations while preserving the ordinal structure used for matching.
Provides exact-recovery and stability guarantees under exact or partial ordinal agreement.
Experiments with frozen encoders show more accurate and stable correspondence recovery under label corruption and domain shift.

papers.abstract: Motivated by ten years of Learning-Based Control Invited Sessions at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), this tutorial paper reviews key advances at the intersection of machine learning and control. We focus on methods that combine the flexibility of machine learning techniques with the structure and theoretical foundations of control to design autonomous systems that are capable, reliable, and safe. We first introduce core notions for establishing stability and safety guarantees, then review approaches that learn dynamics models to improve control under uncertainty, and finally discuss data-driven methods that directly synthesize or learn policies, including reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization. We further discuss representative applications and open challenges. The goal is to provide an accessible entry point to the field and to support continued progress toward reliable learning-based control in real-world systems. To support learning and practical exploration, we share implementations and illustrative examples along with our discussion, together with additional resources on our website: https://learning-based-control.github.io/tutorial/.
bullets: Reviews a decade of learning-based control research presented at IEEE CDC.
Introduces stability and safety concepts for providing formal guarantees.
Covers learned dynamics models for control under uncertainty.
Discusses policy synthesis through reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization.
Includes representative applications, open challenges, implementations, examples, and additional resources.

A PSF does not compute the safe set but certifies safety by a backup trajectory (dotted) into a smaller terminal set Sf .

papers.abstract: Recommender systems often suffer from over-concentrated results when optimized for accuracy, limiting recommendation diversity. While diversity has become an important objective, existing methods still face fundamental limitations from both semantic and structural perspectives. On the one hand, multimodal recommender systems provide rich semantic signals, yet are often treated as auxiliary to ID embeddings, leading to ineffective semantic utilization for diversity. On the other hand, the accuracy--diversity trade-off persists during training, where accuracy gains often come at the cost of diversity. We show that this phenomenon is fundamentally governed by both the structural properties of learned representations and the dynamics of optimization. To address these challenges, we propose MOSS, a unified framework for multimodal decoupling through semantic and structural shaping. Specifically, we first introduce an MLLM-based Decoupled Feature Extraction module to disentangle multimodal content into informative representations. To enhance semantic utilization, we design a Category-aware Embedding Selection module that extracts compact, category-aware semantic features. To address structural limitations, we propose two complementary modules: Alternating Dual-Graph Propagation, which alleviates representation collapse by integrating collaborative and multimodal propagation, and Entropy-based Diversity Regularization, which mitigates optimization bias by promoting balanced category exposure. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MOSS consistently achieves a superior accuracy--diversity trade-off over strong baselines.

Uses MLLM-based decoupled feature extraction and category-aware semantic selection to better exploit multimodal content.
Combines alternating dual-graph propagation with entropy-based regularization to reduce representation collapse and balance category exposure.
Experiments on real-world datasets show a consistently better accuracy–diversity trade-off than strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Retinal fundus images frequently carry more than one disease, and public fundus datasets are heterogeneous and severely long-tailed. Clinical triage suggests a staged design, in which a screening gate, a disease-group router and group-specific classifiers operate in sequence, but it is unclear whether this hierarchy earns its complexity. We present a controlled comparison of three architectures on a unified 39-target label space built from RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0 and ODIR-5K (12,652 images): (i) a three-stage gated cascade of eight models, (ii) a flat model with 39 independent sigmoid outputs, and (iii) a label-correlation model that replaces the flat linear head with 39 learned label queries and a two-layer transformer decoder. All three share one Swin-V2-B backbone, one preprocessing pipeline and one training protocol, so differences are attributable to the architecture. Staging offers no consistent advantage: tracing every missed disease instance to the stage that lost it shows that the two coarse gates discard 34.2% of true instances while the fine-grained classifiers lose only 6.7%, and the gates' hard zeros depress the cascade's macro-AUC to 0.747. Label-correlation modeling gives the largest single gain, raising the detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682 (0.689 with test-time augmentation). Blending the flat and label-correlation models under four-view test-time augmentation is the best configuration on six of eight metrics (exact match 0.694, micro-F1 0.678, macro-F1 0.456, macro-AUC 0.972). On definition-matched class subsets it matches or exceeds four recent studies on macro- and micro-F1, most clearly on low-support pathologies. We also show that ensembling a gated cascade with continuous-output models is harmful, and that per-source negative sampling is needed to remove a dataset shortcut that otherwise yields a spurious AUC of 1.000.

The cascade’s screening gates discard 34.2% of true disease instances, limiting its macro-AUC to 0.747.
Label-correlation modeling improves detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682, or 0.689 with test-time augmentation.

papers.abstract: We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback--Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.
bullets: Targets finetuning with a differentiable reward while maintaining diversity and mode balance.
Uses a time-dependent quadratic control cost: high early to preserve coarse features, low late to refine details.
Is equivalent to reward maximization with time-varying KL regularization over generative paths.
Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and MNIST show a better reward–mode-balance tradeoff than Adjoint Matching.

papers.abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.
bullets: Success depends on both sampling correct answers and whether their upper reward tail beats that of incorrect answers.
Extreme value theory identifies correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical regimes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An illustrative overview of our explanation of BoN for verifiable problems. When n responses are sampled, assuming pass@1 = p, we obtain approximately np correct responses and n(1 − p) incorrect responses, each assigned a reward according to the corresponding reward distribution. Whether BoN selects a correct response is determined by the competition between the maximum reward Mc among the np correct responses and the maximum reward Mw among the n(1− p) incorrect responses. When n is sufficiently large, these maxima are governed by the tails of the respective distributions. Thus, the performance of BoN depends on the competition between the tails of the reward distributions for correct and incorrect responses.

Figure 2: An illustrative explanation of reward hacking in verifiable problems. The blue and orange points represent correct and incorrect sampled responses, respectively, with n points in total. The response outlined in red is the one selected by BoN. Thus, if a blue response is outlined in red, BoN successfully selects a correct response. In the monotonic-improvement case (top row), correct and incorrect responses have reward distributions with the same variance, so their maximum rewards grow at similar rates as n increases. In the reward-hacking case (bottom row), incorrect responses have larger reward variance, causing their maximum reward to grow faster and eventually exceed that of correct responses. Thus, BoN selects a correct response at small n but incorrect one at large n.

papers.abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.
bullets: Addresses weak explanation-quality evaluation and overly coarse graph-context integration in existing methods.
Introduces a rubric measuring faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, validated against human judgments.
Uses progressive disclosure of neighbor records so the language model can focus on fine-grained relevant context.
Trains the graph agent with rubric-guided trajectory distillation for tool use and structured explanation generation.
Shows consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on three fraud datasets under the human-aligned rubric.

papers.abstract: Thermal-to-visible (T2V) face translation has important applications in nighttime biometric recognition, low-light surveillance, and human interpretation of thermal observations. The task remains challenging because thermal images do not directly record visible appearance, while the cross-spectral cues useful for reconstruction vary across frequency components and semantic roles. Existing spatially conditioned models tend to process these cues through a homogeneous adaptation path and do not explicitly separate local structure from global identity. We propose FreqID-Control, a parameter-efficient framework that organizes thermal guidance according to spectral reliability and semantic role while preserving the pretrained generative prior. It combines frequency-routed low-rank adaptation, which allocates separate transformation subspaces to low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail, with shared cross-spectral identity conditioning, which supplies compact global identity tokens independently of spatial thermal tokens. A controlled analysis on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces provides the empirical basis for this design, revealing stable low-frequency correspondence and edge-localized detail correspondence. Experiments on both datasets demonstrate strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation, while controlled ablations on MCXFace confirm the complementary contributions of frequency routing and shared identity conditioning.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reconstructing visible appearance from thermal images, whose useful cues differ by frequency and semantic role.
Uses frequency-routed low-rank adaptation to separately handle low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail while retaining a pretrained generative prior.
Adds shared cross-spectral identity tokens independently from spatial thermal tokens to preserve global facial identity.
Experiments on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces show strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation.
Ablations on MCXFace support complementary benefits from frequency routing and identity conditioning.

papers.abstract: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.
bullets: Models prompts generated by a latent logistic teacher, with the learner inferring the teacher direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples.
Derives an asymptotic test-logit prediction when context length scales with dimension and training prompts scale quadratically with dimension.
Separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable performance factors.
Characterizes effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, sampling temperature, and ridgeless separability.
Predictions closely match finite-dimensional simulations and trained linear-attention models; standard softmax attention shows qualitatively similar behavior outside the theory’s regime.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI), a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy's intrinsic exploration capacity. RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own. Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary. The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr.
bullets: Addresses sparse successful trajectories and training collapse when tasks exceed an agent’s current abilities.
Intervenes during rollout using evaluation rubrics to correct erroneous trajectories.
Filters interventions with excessive distributional shifts so off-policy data can still guide policy optimization.
Across five benchmarks, RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines and approaches the performance of stronger LLMs.
Scope: effectiveness depends on reward-side evidence and controlling distributional shift in intervention trajectories.

papers.abstract: Modern forecasting models are often updated after deployment so they can respond to changing data. These updates can also make predictions worse, so practical systems need a reliable monitor that can detect harmful changes and trigger protection. A natural design is to monitor the same prediction errors that guide the updates. This paper asks whether the statistical guarantee behind such a monitor remains valid when monitoring and adaptation use the same feedback. We study this question in multi-step time-series forecasting. We show that overlapping targets and dependence in forecast errors can break a key assumption required by the guarantee. The monitor may then raise alarms even when no harmful change has occurred, and its response can further damage prediction quality. We also find that adaptation can hide sustained changes from its own monitor, while the original frozen model retains a clearer signal. These results expose a basic failure mode in self-monitored adaptation. They show why reliable deployment requires checking the monitor's assumptions, comparing adaptation with the frozen model under realistic feedback, and limiting the effect of every protective response.
bullets: The paper studies multi-step time-series forecasting systems that adapt after deployment while monitoring the same errors used for adaptation.
Overlapping targets and dependent forecast errors can invalidate exchangeability-based monitoring guarantees.
This may cause false alarms without harmful distribution change, with protective responses further degrading forecasts.
Adaptation can also conceal sustained changes from its own monitor, whereas the frozen model may provide a clearer signal.
Reliable deployment requires validating monitor assumptions, comparing against the frozen model, and limiting protective-response effects.

papers.abstract: The CADENCE algorithm solves the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) with formal coverage and connectivity guarantees, but leaves unspecified which valid corner each agent should be deployed to, a choice that strongly affects efficiency. We introduce two learned corner-selection heuristics that preserve these guarantees: a CNN scoring candidates on a grid encoding, and a GATv2 network trained with Deep Q-Learning (DQN) on a visibility graph. Across 7,500 runs on random orthogonal environments (50x50 to 250x250), our heuristics outperform baseline CADENCE in both steps to full coverage and peak agent count, with gains growing with scale, and improve on Incremental Self-Deployment (ISDA) baselines in agent utilization while providing guarantees ISDA lacks. Learned corner selection thus improves CADENCE in speed and agent utilization at no cost to its formal properties.

Introduces a CNN scorer over grid encodings and a GATv2 network trained with DQN over visibility graphs.
Evaluated across 7,500 random orthogonal environments ranging from 50×50 to 250×250.
Both heuristics reduce steps to full coverage and peak agent count versus CADENCE, with larger gains at larger scales.
They improve agent utilization over ISDA while retaining guarantees that ISDA lacks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal imitation learning requires diverse executable futures under the same observation and consistent behavior across replanning cycles. We present Conditional Trajectory Peaks (CTP), a single-pass policy framework that jointly predicts complete action-chunk candidates, probability masses, and trajectory scales. Distribution-Aware Peak Specialization (DAPS) specializes trajectory peaks using trajectory-level posterior responsibilities and mass- and scale-modulated overlap constraints. Evidence-Gated Trajectory Belief Transport (ETBT) maintains cross-chunk consistency through geometric correspondence between exchangeable candidate sets, while allowing current policy evidence to override historical constraints. CTP achieves a coverage score of 91.40% on Push-T; success rates of 100.0%, 79.72%, and 84.44% on D3IL Avoiding, Aligning, and Sorting-2, respectively. On LIBERO, CTP achieves an average success rate of 97.25%. In real-world dual-arm experiments, CTP preserves both placement modes in a two-plate task, succeeding in all 50 trials. On bottle uprighting and pen placement into a holder, it maintains success rates comparable to $π_{0.5}$ while reducing policy inference latency from 218.24 ms to 75.80 ms. These results demonstrate that single-pass trajectory modeling can combine multimodal behavior, closed-loop consistency, and efficient inference.
bullets: Jointly predicts complete action-chunk candidates, their probability masses, and trajectory scales.
Uses DAPS to specialize trajectory peaks through posterior responsibilities and mass- and scale-aware overlap constraints.
Uses ETBT to transport trajectory beliefs across chunks while allowing current evidence to override past constraints.
Reports strong simulated and real-world performance, including 97.25% average success on LIBERO and 50/50 success in a two-plate task.
Reduces inference latency from 218.24 ms to 75.80 ms while retaining comparable success to π₀.₅ on bottle uprighting and pen placement.

papers.abstract: An agent deployed in a single body cannot learn how fast that body wears, because every trial that would reveal its wear resistance wears the body it would protect. We study this \emph{epoch-one} setting, in which the parameters of a fixed-weight policy are set before the body is drawn and never updated in life. The agent carries a load-gated nociceptive channel and a memory that retains what was felt. We prove that felt cost moves the allocation to the best-\emph{paid} work not yet felt rather than the gentlest, that an agent without retention never sees the felt-cost constraint bind, and that the channel pays only where the threat is individually unpredictable, cheap to avoid and expensive to ignore. We measure per body, setting the agent with channel and memory against the same individual without them, where neither carries a schedule learned across lives. On $2{,}000$ simulated floor-layer knees, with wear anchored to published loss rates, feeling, retaining and substituting extends the working life from age $55.2$ to $59.6$ and raises career output from $33.7$ to $36.1$. $69.3\%$ of bodies gain and \textbf{none lose}. A body that feels but retains nothing past the day gains one of the $+4.4$ years, and retention carries the rest. A population-trained agent gains $+0.65$ years from the same channel at $-0.54$ output. The difference is what a species prior already supplies, and a single body has none. The two are related by an identity, the ablation mean reporting $(1-χ)$ of the per-body value with $χ$ the share a blind schedule already captures, so we report both. Where the regime map predicts value, a care robot sextuples its certified service life and a field-anchored fleet writes off $0.15$ of its machines instead of $0.55$. Where it predicts none, a rover gains little over blind caution, so the map holds in both directions.

Combines a load-gated nociceptive channel with memory of experienced costs to guide work allocation and avoidance.

Memory provides most of the benefit: feeling without retaining adds 1 of the 4.4 years gained, while retention supplies the remainder.
A regime map predicts where nociception helps, with reported gains in care robots and field fleets but little benefit for rovers in regimes favoring blind caution.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach to training language model agents, but sparse and delayed outcome rewards provide limited guidance for credit assignment across long interaction sequences. Recent work on on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers complementary supervision by evaluating a policy's sampled responses under privileged training-time context. However, our diagnostics show that positive average agreement between outcome and hindsight feedback coexists with substantial local disagreement, raising the question of how to allocate influence between them at each decision. We introduce UniOPSD (Unified On-Policy Self-Distillation), which unifies these feedback sources through adaptive local credit arbitration. UniOPSD constructs comparable credit estimates from environmental returns and successful-peer hindsight at shared interaction anchors. Historical agreement determines the global mixing level, while current signal availability and relative precision adjust each source's influence at individual decisions. The episode-level outcome contribution is retained, and bounded token modulation refines the fused step credit for policy optimization. With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, UniOPSD achieves ALFWorld success rates of $82.8\%$ and $83.6\%$, WebShop success rates of $75.0\%$ and $82.0\%$, and Search-QA aggregate accuracies of $45.3\%$ and $49.8\%$, respectively. On 3B WebShop, UniOPSD improves over SDAR by $7.0$ percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zenghuang-Fu/Uniopsd

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) offer visual foresight for robotic manipulation, but pixel-space models repeatedly reconstruct entire future scenes, incurring high computational cost and spatio-temporal redundancy. In physical manipulation, consecutive frames often share most of their visual context; the changes between them are what an action policy needs to anticipate. We introduce DeltaWAM, a change-centric WAM that makes a compact delta token the unit of future prediction. Each token is a single vector encoding changes between consecutive dense DINO feature maps. DeltaWAM builds on DeltaWorld, a latent world model pretrained on large-scale videos, to autoregressively predict one delta token per future frame. A flow-matching action expert then conditions on the predicted transitions and current DINO features, which serve as spatial anchors, to generate action chunks. Trained for 256 GPU hours on two H100 GPUs, DeltaWAM has 0.725B parameters and achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO. It also shows robust generalization under procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro. Inference takes 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory.
bullets: Addresses the redundancy and computational expense of reconstructing entire future scenes in visual foresight.
Represents each frame transition as a single delta token derived from consecutive dense DINO feature maps.
Uses DeltaWorld for autoregressive delta prediction and a flow-matching action expert conditioned on predicted changes and current visual anchors.
Achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO and robust generalization to procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro.

papers.abstract: We present FloodDiffusion 2 (FD2), an efficient and controllable framework that builds upon FloodDiffusion (FD1), a state-of-the-art streaming motion generation model. While FD1 produces plausible motion, it suffers from low efficiency and limited controllability, as its attention design requires repeated computation over the entire history, and it lacks precise trajectory control for real-world applications. To address these limitations and improve generation quality, FD2 introduces three advances. First, Partial Attention makes finalized history representations independent of the active window, enabling KV-cached inference and shared-history packing for efficient training. Second, we establish a necessary-and-sufficient Bregman criterion for regression losses to preserve diffusion's conditional-mean velocity field. This criterion guides an FK-induced quadratic loss that incorporates motion geometry without online FK evaluation. Third, FD2 introduces precise path conditioning to control the character's root trajectory while preserving natural body motion. Experiments show that FD2 reduces training computation by 4.6$\times$ and accelerates denoising by 11.29$\times$, reaching 2.303 ms per update on long sequences. Alongside these efficiency gains, FD2 improves motion quality over FD1 and achieves state-of-the-art FID scores among streaming methods, with 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.
bullets: Targets FD1’s repeated-history computation and limited trajectory control.

Adds precise root-path conditioning while preserving natural full-body motion.

papers.abstract: Latent generative models make 3D medical image synthesis computationally practical by generating in a compressed space. However, we show that the common flat Euclidean assumption induced by $\ell_2$ objectives is imprecise: latent-space geometry is so strongly anisotropic that equal-magnitude errors can produce drastically different decoded distortions. We further find that this anisotropy has a clear feature: sensitive variation concentrates in a low-rank subspace. The dominant low-rank components capture the overall structure, encoding long-range, spatially coordinated variation while remaining resistant to local noise. Its orthogonal residual, in contrast, mainly captures local and image-specific variation. Motivated by this asymmetry, we introduce Latent Structure Flow (LSF). At each block, LSF decomposes the latent state into structure and residual, models structural changes with global context, and predicts residual variation locally while preserving a direct path for the input structure. LSF changes only the generator, leaving the frozen codec and pointwise training objective unchanged. Across cross-modality synthesis and tumor inpainting tasks, LSF outperforms all compared baselines on both global and tumor-specific metrics, demonstrating the benefit of explicitly modeling latent-space structure for 3D medical image synthesis.
bullets: The common flat Euclidean assumption for latent spaces can misrepresent decoded image distortions because sensitivity is direction-dependent.
Sensitive variation concentrates in a low-rank subspace capturing coordinated, long-range structure; the orthogonal residual captures local, image-specific details.
Latent Structure Flow (LSF) decomposes latent states into structure and residual, modeling them with global and local context respectively.
LSF modifies only the generator while keeping the codec frozen and the pointwise training objective unchanged.
Across cross-modality synthesis and tumor inpainting, LSF outperforms the compared baselines on global and tumor-specific metrics.

papers.abstract: Large-scale point cloud representations of complex geome tries incur prohibitive computational and memory costs, necessitating compressed implicit representations. To ad dress this, we propose a unified framework comprising im plicit geometric field representation, hierarchical frequency domain compression, and conditional high-frequency predic tion. Specifically, an unordered point cloud is mapped to an implicit field defined within its physical bounding box. A smooth Fourier pyramid is then constructed, where com pact low-frequency components capture the global geometry. Inter-scale high-frequency residuals are encoded to preserve the spatial information required for reconstructing fine geo metric details. To restore the high-frequency information lost during compression, we develop a hierarchical 3D neural net work. The reconstructed implicit field is converted back into a point cloud through isosurface extraction. Experiments on a complex-boundary point cloud with more than eight mil lion points demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a higher compression ratio than existing point cloud compres sion methods while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality.
bullets: Maps unordered point clouds to implicit fields within their physical bounding boxes.
Uses a smooth Fourier pyramid to retain global geometry in low frequencies and encode fine details as inter-scale high-frequency residuals.
Employs a hierarchical 3D neural network to predict missing high-frequency information after compression.
Reconstructs point clouds from the recovered implicit field through isosurface extraction.
On a point cloud exceeding eight million points, achieves a higher compression ratio than existing methods with comparable reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Reconstruct where the images provide evidence, and generate where they do not: recent success of spatial world models such as Atlas (World Labs Team, 2026) highlights the value of unifying reconstruction and generation in one model. Yet the two have long lived in separate paradigms with distinctive failure modes: feed-forward reconstruction averages ambiguity into blur, while conditional generation invents plausible but scene-inconsistent detail. In this work, we present a unified flow-based formulation for reconstruction and generation, where a shared clean-target predictor performs direct reconstruction at its single-step endpoint and unfolds conditional generation through multi-step flow. A controlled toy study reveals the mechanism: with a single step, the predictor collapses to the conditional mean just like feed-forward methods, favoring consistency over diversity. With multi-step inference, the fidelity of generated details grows with context richness: closer observations reduce ambiguity and yield better-matched details. We further instantiate the formulation in appearance and geometry 3D tasks. JiT-LVSM improves perceptual and distributional quality in novel view synthesis, while JUSt3R retains competitive single-step geometry prediction with additional multi-step inference capabilities that reduces veil and flying-pixel artifacts, producing cleaner surface structure with greater test-time compute. Together, they show that reconstruction and generation can share both a formulation and a backbone, with their behavior governed by denoising configuration---making unification surprisingly simple.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between blurry feed-forward reconstruction and scene-inconsistent conditional generation.
Uses a shared clean-target predictor: direct reconstruction at one step, conditional generation through multi-step flow.
A toy study shows single-step inference approaches the conditional mean, while richer context improves multi-step detail fidelity.
Applied to 3D appearance and geometry tasks, the approach improves novel-view quality and reduces veil and flying-pixel artifacts.
The formulation shares both backbone and behavior across tasks, with the denoising configuration controlling the reconstruction–generation trade-off.

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve increasingly diverse reasoning tasks, yet their performance remains highly sensitive to task prompts, intermediate instructions, and the way reusable problem-solving knowledge is incorporated. Existing optimization methods usually focus on only one part of this design space: they either optimize a monolithic prompt, or separately induce and refine skills from model traces. As a result, they lack a principled mechanism for deciding which component should be updated when failures occur, and they rarely optimize prompts, skills, and skill-use policies in a unified framework. We propose SPARO (Skill, Prompt, And Routing Optimization), a framework that jointly optimizes task instructions, reusable skill blocks, and routing rules. It performs controlled counterfactual evaluations, converts examples' effects into a probabilistic responsibility distribution over prompt, skill, and routing components, samples one component from that distribution, and applies the corresponding targeted mutation. This design moves language-program optimization beyond global prompt rewriting toward structured, reusable, and selectively activated task knowledge. Across five benchmarks and five worker models, SPARO consistently outperforms both prompt-centered and skill-centered optimization baselines. These results suggest that effective language-program optimization depends not only on discovering useful task knowledge, but also on deciding where that knowledge should be stored and when it should be activated.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of methods that optimize only prompts or skills independently.
Uses counterfactual evaluations to estimate each component’s probabilistic responsibility for example outcomes.
Samples a prompt, skill, or routing component for targeted mutation based on that attribution.

Highlights that optimization requires deciding both where knowledge is stored and when it is activated.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors (VBTS) provide rich contact information for robotic manipulation, but existing designs can be hard to simplify and adapt to the size and constraints of humanoid fingertips. We introduce \textbf{GlowTact}, a pressure-responsive vision-based tactile sensing mechanism that directly visualizes contact pressure. \textbf{GlowTact} requires only single-color, non-directional illumination, and the raw tactile image directly represents the pressure distribution without explicit geometry reconstruction. This simple sensing principle enables compact, customizable tactile sensors while preserving high sensitivity and rich spatial detail. We demonstrate gram-scale contact detection, accurate normal-force estimation, and reconstruction of fine contact geometry, including M1 screw threads. These results establish \textbf{GlowTact} as a practical new sensing technology for compact humanoid fingertips, combining a durable nitrile membrane and simple optical design with sensitive and information-rich tactile perception.
bullets: Targets the complexity and size constraints of tactile sensors for humanoid fingertips.
Uses a pressure-responsive mechanism with non-directional, single-color illumination.
Produces raw tactile images that directly encode pressure distributions without geometry reconstruction.
Demonstrates gram-scale contact detection, normal-force estimation, and fine contact-geometry reconstruction, including M1 screw threads.
Combines a durable nitrile membrane with a simple optical design for compact, information-rich sensing.

papers.abstract: Human-robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world-state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human-robot interaction.
bullets: Frames diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) rather than isolated technical faults.
Combines multimodal perception, IoT-based digital augmentation, and an LLM to expose assumptions, classify mismatch types, and identify needed verification evidence.

A second LLM call (LLM-Revise) revises the hypothesis conditioned on grounded evidence, after which supported mismatch types are filtered and a primary type is selected via precedence-based adjudication.

The robot’s verification indicates that the cup does not contain enough water, which conflicts with the human’s assumed world state implied by the instruction (i.e., the water is sufficient). The system therefore identifies a World-State Mismatch (WSM) and informs the user (“Not enough water left”). The robot asks whether it should add some water or deliver other beverage instead. With IoT-enabled WSM detection, the robot checks indoor air quality, outdoor AQI, pollen, weather, noise, and device status, and then selects a safer alternative such as an air purifier or fresh-air system when outdoor conditions are poor. In Scenario 2, the user asks the robot to hang clothes on the balcony, implicitly assuming that the balcony will remain suitable for drying. Without IoT, the robot may hang the clothes outside because it is not raining at the moment. papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is typically framed as learning a direct mapping from historical to future observations in the observation space. However, sequences of observations generally provide only a partial view of the dynamics of the underlying system, with future observations being shaped by latent dynamics. Recent latent-space forecasting methods thus achieve improved performance by predicting future observations from latent-space representations of historical observations rather than directly forecasting future observations in the observation space. Next, while future observations are also shaped by external factors, how to incorporate external, often multimodal, information into forecasting, so that it can shape latent-state formation and evolution directly, remains underexplored. We propose WorldTS, a world-modeling based forecasting framework that integrates multimodal covariates directly into the forecasting to further improve forecasting performance. Specifically, WorldTS employs a two-stage training strategy. First, it learns forecasting-relevant latent state dynamics conditioned on multimodal covariates, yielding encoded future states. Next, the learned state dynamics are frozen, and an observation decoder is trained to map the predicted future states back to future observations. Extensive experiments on 21 real-world datasets offer insight into WorldTS and its effectiveness.

Uses a two-stage world-modeling framework to learn covariate-conditioned latent state dynamics and decode them into future observations.

Then freezes the learned dynamics and trains an observation decoder to reconstruct future observations.

papers.abstract: Recent empirical and theoretical advances suggest that joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) may learn meaningful representations for action-conditioned prediction of future outcomes, thus becoming one of the foundational structures for world models. However, accurate prediction does not, in general, necessarily imply recovery of underlying causal states that give rise to the observed dynamics. This work investigates when and how JEPAs can recover the underlying causal states from observations. We first introduce a latent variable model, in which high-dimensional observations are generated from latent causal states whose dynamics are governed by action-conditioned transition mechanisms. Based on this formulation, we develop a general information-theoretic objective that combines conditional likelihood maximization for learning transition dynamics with entropy maximization for preserving latent state information. We then establish identifiability conditions under which representations learned by this general objective recover the underlying latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation. One key condition for such identifiability is sufficient action-induced variation in the transition mechanisms. Guided by this finding, we instantiate the general objective with an action-modulated Gaussian additive-noise model, yielding action-modulated JEPA (A-JEPA). Experiments on synthetic environments verify the theoretical findings under the identifiability conditions and robustness to moderate violations, while visual benchmarks demonstrate improved state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms.
bullets: Motivation: Accurate action-conditioned prediction does not necessarily reveal the causal states underlying observed dynamics.
Method: Formulates a latent causal-state model and combines conditional transition-likelihood maximization with entropy maximization to preserve state information.
Theory: Derives identifiability conditions allowing recovery of latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation.
Key condition: Actions must induce sufficient variation in the transition mechanisms.
Results: A-JEPA validates the theory in synthetic environments and improves state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms on visual benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to localize the spatio-temporal tube in a video corresponding to a natural language query. While recent methods achieve strong performance in fully supervised, weakly supervised, and zero-shot settings, they typically rely on computationally expensive architectures, complex training pipelines, or multimodal large language models. We present Pocket-STVG (P-STVG), a lightweight cascade architecture that addresses STVG by combining efficient pre-trained components instead of large end-to-end models. P-STVG integrates a temporal-aware video encoder based on MobileViCLIP, a spatial encoder-decoder derived from MDETR, and a shared aligned text encoder. Temporal localization is performed through either a lightweight 1D U-Net or a simple thresholding strategy, enabling the same framework to operate in both weakly supervised and zero-shot settings. Furthermore, video representations are precomputed independently of the query, yielding an indexing-friendly pipeline for efficient inference and large-scale video collections. Despite requiring fewer than 90M parameters, P-STVG performs on par with weakly supervised methods and improves on earlier zero-shot approaches at a fraction of their memory and computational cost, establishing a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off for STVG.
